The opening tutorial had me thrilled. The aesthetic and potential seemed very high. I was excited to use these systems to solve some cases.

The Operator is a narrative-driven game where you step into the role of an FDI Agent, solving criminal cases by analyzing evidence, searching databases, and assisting field agents.

The game gives you the illusion of meaningful choices, but in reality it's a fairly linear experience. No matter what decisions you make, the story ultimately follows the same path. If you're expecting multiple endings or a branching narrative where your choices have lasting consequences, you may end up disappointed.

That said, if you're looking for an engaging, story-focused experience to relax with on a lazy Sunday afternoon, The Operator absolutely delivers. The investigations are entertaining, the atmosphere is great, and the gameplay does a good job of making you feel like you're working behind the scenes as an investigator. As long as you go in expecting an interactive story rather than a true choice-driven adventure, you'll likely have a great time.

The game is brief, with frustrating mechanics, obvious plot from the start and feels super lacking in choices mattering at all. Overall one-dimensional, predetermined path you must play "correctly" and just see the events unfold in the only way possible. There is absolutely no freedom, second path or any autonomy at any point - just like entering the credentials - you just need to type anything and watch the correct letters appear - so is the game deciding what you do and where you end up, the only point of failure available - a bomb defusal that you can replay and read a frustrating long manual with no back button for absolutely no plot or artistic reason over and over. I played this on my steam deck and the hours didn't transfer over, but I did complete it and highly recommend. Don't get me wrong, it's an interesting story and the final plot twist is one I definitely didn't expect. The UI and the mechanics were interesting, and while it wasn't very hard at least I didn't have to ask for help so it's pretty easy access for people who aren't hardcore into mystery solving. However, I feel like this concept could have gone SO much further- the open ending could have allowed for at least twice as much story and overall I feel like the whole Operator thing should have lasted longer- either been stretched out more in time (because timeline wise this all happens VERY fast) or just... had more to do, more characters to meet? It's supposed to be a full time job and yet we practically only help with a single case a day. In short, I'll repeat what I've seen a lot of other reviews say; this game had a lot of potential. I almost feel like this could be a demo! I bought it on sale, so it's fine, but for a game that has practically only three hours of gameplay I feel like the price (while probably very justified for the developers), isn't really worth it for people with limited funds, especially since there's no real replayability. If you have the money to spare, sure, it's a fun but short game that isn't too hard, but if you want some challenge or you're trying to figure out what to spend your limited allowance on, this probably isn't it.

The Operator is somewhat summed up as an detective esk simulator game where the bulk of the gamelay loop is behind your desk, gathering evidence & solving cases by connecting the dots. It was clearly inspired by games such as Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You, Song of Farca and the likes, so if that's up your alley you'll most likely also enjoy this one.

Though: an unfortunate difference between those games and this one is both the depth & usage of the built in systems/tools at your disposal, the very linear story, and the playtime of the game. Starting with the latter, a normal playthrough of the game sits around 2 to 3 hours. As the game is very linear in terms of choices you can make (the choices only change a few minor responses, there is only a singular ending and your choices don't affect this) there is not really a great reason to replay the game unless you're going for all achievements; as some are missable on a first playthrough.

Which makes the price, +-14EUR (without sale, as of writing this), a complicated point.

Apart from the playtime, the game makes up for it by the amazing voice acting (not AI generated), _amazing_ polished look and feel (you can clearly see a lot of love and thought were poured into this) and really interesting scenes (artistic direction wise) splattered between days. All in all, really good experience and amazing opener; especially for an indie developer. (there are some minor complaints such as the chat stealing your focus when having to make a choice preventing you from typing in a different window, but nothing game breaking.) -- Just in the end wished with this much work & love put into it, the story was a tad longer.

My final gripe was the somewhat limited use and complexity of the tools given to you. It goes hand in hand with the point about playtime, because how else would you utilize a lab analysis tool or terminal if not by expanding the story. There were tools that looked really interesting, but are in the end just used once; which is a shame really. The times you do utilize them are fun and all feel unique.

So. All in all, a really solid game that I see more so as a foundation for something bigger. It at times feels more like a demo than an full game story wise. If you don't mind the price for what you're getting, and games like orwell are up your alley; you'll enjoy this one. But it may be better to wait for the operator 2 (which is currently in development!) or play a similar game if you're looking for a longer story or if you don't prefer the linear story style of this game.

Has promise, but doesn't deliver.

Mechanically there are a handful of things that seem interesting and like you should pay attention to them that just don't go anywhere. There is no real point in taking notes because you are handed solutions to every problem without needing to look around or remember anything.

Cool, I can run programs from my terminal - [spoiler] e.g. I can call certain people if I pay attention to their IP addresses [/spoiler]. But does that come up at all after I'm shown it? No, it's a one-off to get my to type something into the terminal for vibes. Problems are not solveable outside of the linear storyline. Problems and solutions are presented to you side by side. There is no payoff for paying attention to details, because they don't go anywhere, you can't use them to figure anything out. Very much on rails, and a disappointing detective game experience. I almost thought this would go somewhere cool at the end [spoiler] and that you would continue the game as HAL and actually find out who the mysterious baddies are [/spoiler], but this too does not pay off. Just leaves me wanting more, but not in a good way; feels almost like a demo. When it was revealed [spoiler] who the mole was I was like yeah, ok, there are like 6 total people I have met who aren't dead, of course it's my sketchy friend Mike who's been acting weird. [/spoiler]

That being said, individual minigames and puzzles were genuinely fun to solve. I wish the game leaned more into the mechanics and systems they had, I think that is where they were strongest, and made it important and useful to take notes - reward paying attention to the details! Why give us a notepad if there's nothing you realistically need to write down? I wish I like this game more!

Now the bad.  Sorry for the spoilers, but the end is just so bad.  The between shift cutscenes (if you call super blurred nonsense a cutscene) were a total waste other than to give a sound cue to solve an end game puzzle and to make the answer to that puzzle not immediately obvious. I dunno if they were going for dark and edgy or if they wanted something that would happen in real life, but either way I play games for the illusion that good guys can win. Ended up not enjoying this one. Pros: spiffy interface, interesting connect-the-dots puzzles, and a very nice hint system that preserves immersion in the story. Cons: too short, way too much text to read as another person is typing it, and the final sequences sort of blast out of nowhere. A decent puzzle game with some great moments and other bits that dragged a little. My favourite parts were the bomb scare scene, and also the chemical analyses, though I may be a little biased in that regard. I largely found the dialogue engaging, especially with Walker, though I felt as though Tanner sometimes suffered for not having a voice. The puzzles were largely pretty content to hold your hand, which I think could have been adjusted a little, perhaps with a difficulty setting for how much work the programs you use do for you. At times not being able to skip dialogue weighed it down, though I acknowledge that I'm a fast reader and thus have a bad habit of reading the dialogue text and getting impatient waiting for the voice actor to catch up. Largely, great voice acting. Honestly, aside from the sometimes unchallenging nature of the puzzles, the story was the biggest thorn for me. The number of twists I saw coming, telegraphed as twists by the music, meant that I was less able to appreciate the reveal at the end, which I didn't put together as I played this over a rather long timeframe and parts had faded from my memory, allowing the potential for the "oh shit" moment as everything recontextualises, but it was so undercut by other reveals that I did expect that what should've been a great moment was somewhat glossed over. Together with the fact that the ending felt sudden, I thought that there wasn't enough time to feel as Tanner/ Cole would, killing the emotional weight. Overall, a nice little brain teaser, despite its flaws, and I look forward to what the developer makes next
